Per-residue deconvolution of HDX-MS uptake from overlapping peptides

Source: R/residue_deconvolution.R
residue_deconvolution.Rd

Estimates a single-residue-resolution deuterium uptake profile from overlapping peptide-level data, by solving a constrained least-squares problem rather than simply averaging peptides that cover a residue. Each peptide's observed uptake (in Daltons) is modelled as the sum of the per-residue uptake of every exchangeable residue it covers (the first two residues of each peptide and all non-first Prolines are excluded, matching the convention used in nb_exch_deut()). The resulting system is solved per Protein State, replicate, and timepoint with residue-level uptake constrained to \[0, 1\] (a residue cannot be less than fully protected or more than fully deuterated). With typical overlapping-peptide coverage (redundancy > ~5x), this recovers sharper, more localized residue-level resolution than a plain per-residue mean across covering peptides, particularly at region boundaries where long peptides would otherwise blend signal from neighboring residues into a region's apparent value.

Usage

residue_deconvolution(df, protein_length, lambda_smooth = 0.1)

Arguments

df

data.frame, output of output_tp() called with percent = FALSE. Uptake in Daltons is required because it is additive across residues; percent deuteration is not (it depends on each peptide's own number of exchangeable residues) and cannot be used directly for deconvolution.

protein_length

integer, total number of residues in the protein. Used to set the residue index range for the deconvolution.

lambda_smooth

non-negative numeric, default 0.1. Strength of an L2 penalty on the difference between adjacent covered residues (only applied between residues that are actually consecutive in sequence - a gap in coverage breaks the chain). 0 reproduces the original, unregularized per-timepoint fit. Larger values pull neighboring residues toward the same value unless the peptide data specifically distinguish them. The default of 0.1 is a modest starting point, not a universally correct value - the right strength depends on peptide redundancy and protein size. On the example data, values between 0 and 1 predicted left-out peptides equally well.

Value

data.frame with one row per residue and Deut.Time, and one column per Protein.State/replicate (same naming as the X..Deut columns in df), giving the deconvolved per-residue fractional uptake (0-1). Residues not covered by any peptide at a given timepoint are NA.

What it does not do

Each time point is solved on its own. There is no kinetic model and no link between time points. lambda_smooth > 0 adds a penalty on the difference between neighboring residues within one time point.

See also

nb_exch_deut(), output_tp(), coverage_residue(), residue_level_average()

Examples

file_nm <- system.file("extdata", "All_results_table.csv", package = "HDXBoxeR")
a <- output_tp(file_nm, percent = FALSE)
#> Protein.States used: Unbound bound
#> Deut.times used: 3.00s 60.00s 1800.00s 72000.00s
#> 29 peptide row(s) dropped: 29 not measured in every state, 0 with fewer than 2 replicate value(s)
#> Number of replicates used: Unbound=3 bound=3
#> no csv file written
res <- residue_deconvolution(a, protein_length = 225)
res_unsmoothed <- residue_deconvolution(a, protein_length = 225, lambda_smooth = 0)
